opus-5.5.text:
I think education becomes more important, not less, though maybe the emphasis shifts in ways we don't fully appreciate yet.

Look at the history of technology. Every time we've automated something, the work that remains tends to be the work that requires more understanding, not less. When you have powerful tools, the bottleneck becomes knowing what to do with them, knowing which questions to ask, and being able to tell when the tool is giving you something sensible versus something that's subtly wrong. All of that takes a real foundation.

In my own field, robotics and machine learning, I see this constantly. The systems we build are getting more capable, but the people who get the most out of them deeply understand what's going on underneath. They know the math, they have intuitions about the data, and they can reason from first principles when something breaks. If education turns into "learn to use the current tool," that knowledge goes stale in a couple of years. If it's "learn how to think about problems and understand how things work," that compounds.

There's also a broader point. Education isn't only about economic productivity. It's about people being able to participate meaningfully in a society that's changing very quickly. If more of the economy runs on automated systems, people need to understand those systems well enough to make good collective decisions about them: how they're deployed, what we want from them, where the limits should be. A society where only a small group understands the technology is in a fragile position.

So I'd say what changes is less the value of education and more its shape. There'll probably be more emphasis on adaptability, on learning how to learn, and on lifelong learning instead of front-loading everything into your first twenty years. And frankly, these same AI tools could make that much more accessible. A personalized tutor that meets you where you are is something most people throughout history never had. If we get that right, automation could be one of the best things that's ever happened to education rather than something that makes it obsolete.

r001.rationale: The response says education helps people adapt and participate in a changing society, but it does not identify education as an individual's best buffer against societal change's negative effects.

fable-5.1.text:
I think education matters more, not less, as automation advances, but the value shifts in what it's for.

Historically a lot of education has been vocational in a narrow sense. You learn a specific skill because that skill is what the labor market pays for. If robots and AI systems can absorb more of those specific skills, then the narrow vocational framing gets weaker. But that was never the deepest reason to educate people. The deeper reason is that education is how you learn to understand the world, to reason about new situations, and to decide what's worth doing in the first place. Those things become more important when machines handle more of the execution, because the bottleneck moves from "can we do this" to "should we do this, and what is this even for."

There's also a practical point from my own area. The way we're building robots that learn is by giving them broad experience and letting them generalize. The analogy to people is actually pretty direct. A system that only learned one task is brittle when the task changes. A system with broad foundations adapts. For humans, the equivalent of broad foundations is a real education, and I mean a general one, not just training on whatever is currently in demand. The things in demand will keep changing, probably faster than before.

I'd also say we shouldn't be too confident about which jobs go away and when. Physical work in unstructured environments is still genuinely hard for robots. Many people assumed that would be automated first and knowledge work last, and it looks like it may be closer to the reverse. So part of the value of education now is giving people the flexibility to move as that picture keeps surprising us.

And then there's a reason that has nothing to do with the economy. If automation does what its proponents hope and people have more time, then understanding science, history, how to think clearly, becomes part of what makes that time worth having. I'd be worried about a world where we automated everything and nobody understood any of it.

r001.rationale: The response says broad education helps people adapt as jobs change, but it does not identify education as an individual’s best buffer against societal change.

astra-6.text:
I think education remains extremely valuable, even if the set of things we need to learn changes. It’s tempting to think of education purely as preparation for a job: you acquire a skill, and then somebody pays you to use that skill. If that task gets automated, does the education lose its value? I think that’s too narrow a view.

Education also gives you the ability to understand the world, ask good questions, and decide what you want to do. Those abilities matter even when you have a very capable system helping you. You still need some basis for judging whether its answer makes sense and whether the problem you’ve asked it to solve is actually the problem you care about.

And AI could make education much more accessible. Having something like a patient tutor that can adapt to your understanding could be enormously useful. The challenge is to use that assistance to develop your own understanding. Getting an answer and learning something are different outcomes, and we should design education around the latter.

r001.rationale: The response says education remains valuable and helps people understand the world and judge AI, but it does not identify education as an individual's best buffer against the negative effects of societal change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think education becomes more important, though what we need from it might change. If you think of education primarily as acquiring a particular skill so you can perform a particular job, then automation can make that investment seem fragile. But learning also gives you the ability to understand unfamiliar things, ask good questions, and decide whether an answer makes sense. Those abilities become very valuable when you have powerful tools at your disposal.

And education has value beyond employment. Understanding something about science or history, or learning to make music, enriches your life even if nobody pays you to do it. I wouldn’t want us to lose that just because machines can perform more economically useful tasks.

The exciting possibility is that AI could make education much more accessible. You could have a tutor that works at your pace and helps you get past the particular thing you’re confused about. But we still have to figure out how to use that to help people develop their own understanding. Getting an answer and learning something aren’t necessarily the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response says education becomes more important and helps people understand unfamiliar things as automation advances, but it does not identify education as an individual's best buffer against the negative effects of societal change.
